blocks.content: Entities on their own are just a pile of classes. What turns them into a system is how they connect. Relationships describe who owns whom, who uses whom, and who is a kind of whom.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782974116196-612582780.png
Once you have your entities, ask a simple question about each pair: how do these two relate? The answers turn a loose list of classes into a real, working design.

blocks.title: The two magic questions
blocks.content: For any pair of entities, ask "is a" or "has a". Those two questions unlock almost every relationship you will ever need to model.
1. Why Relationships Matter
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972218059-593190215.png
blocks.alt: The four kinds of relationship between classes

blocks.content: Relationships decide how your classes reference each other, and getting them right keeps the whole design clean and flexible.

["They show which class holds a reference to which other class.","They reveal ownership, like a parking lot owning its slots.","They guide where behaviour and data should live.","They shape how the design grows when new features arrive."]
items: They show which class holds a reference to which other class.
They reveal ownership, like a parking lot owning its slots.
They guide where behaviour and data should live.
They shape how the design grows when new features arrive.

blocks.content: The Two Big Questions: Is A and Has A
blocks.text: The Two Big Questions: Is A and Has A

blocks.content: Almost every relationship is one of these two. Learn to ask both for every pair of entities.
Is a: inheritance
When one entity is a specialised kind of another, that is an is a relationship, modelled with inheritance. A Car is a Vehicle. A Truck is a Vehicle.
Has a: association, aggregation, composition
When one entity contains or uses another, that is a has a relationship. A ParkingLot has Slots. A Ticket has a Vehicle. Most relationships are some form of has a.
Start every pair with these two questions. Is a Car a Vehicle? That is inheritance. Does a ParkingLot have Slots? That is has a.
2. Association: One Class Uses Another
The loosest link. One class simply uses another, without owning it. Neither controls the other lifetime.
Association is common for temporary interactions, like a service using a repository, where the two are related but independent.
Aggregation: Has A, But Can Live Alone
blocks.text: Aggregation: Has A, But Can Live Alone

blocks.content: A stronger has a, where one entity holds another, but the held part can exist on its own even without the whole.
Aggregation says "this belongs with that, loosely". The part is shared or independent, and it does not vanish when the whole is gone.
3. Composition: Has A, And Owns Its Life
blocks.text: 3. Composition: Has A, And Owns Its Life

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972219795-522098402.png
blocks.alt: A house owns its rooms, they die with it

blocks.content: The strongest has a. The part cannot live without the whole. When the whole is destroyed, so are its parts.
Composition says "this is truly part of that". A parking lot owns its slots, a house owns its rooms. The parts have no meaning on their own.
Aggregation vs Composition
These two confuse many candidates, so here is the clean difference side by side.

{"headers":["Aspect","Aggregation","Composition"],"rows":[["Ownership","Loose, shared","Strong, exclusive"],["Lifetime","Part outlives the whole","Part dies with the whole"],["Example","Team and Players","House and Rooms"]]}

blocks.title: The lifetime test
blocks.content: Ask: if I destroy the whole, should the part survive? If yes, it is aggregation. If no, it is composition.
4. Inheritance: Is A
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972221337-916793701.png
blocks.alt: Car and Truck are kinds of Vehicle

blocks.content: When one entity is genuinely a kind of another, they share common behaviour through inheritance. The child gets the parent fields and methods, and adds its own.
Inheritance is powerful, but it is also the most overused relationship in interviews. Use it only for a true is a, never just to share a little code.
5. Prefer Composition Over Inheritance
This is one of the most valuable principles in object oriented design. When unsure between is a and has a, lean toward has a.

Inheritance locks a child tightly to its parent, and deep inheritance chains become fragile: a change high up can break everything below. Composition, holding another object and delegating to it, stays flexible.

blocks.title: A tempting but wrong inheritance
blocks.text: Making Stack extend ArrayList feels easy, but now Stack exposes list methods that break its rules. Better: Stack has a list inside and exposes only push and pop.

blocks.content: Favour has a over is a when in doubt. Composition bends where inheritance breaks.
6. Multiplicity: How Many?
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972223053-558224545.png
blocks.alt: One to one, one to many, and many to many

blocks.content: Relationships also carry a count, called multiplicity. Ask how many of one relate to how many of the other, because it decides whether you store a single reference or a list.
["One to one: a ticket maps to one vehicle.","One to many: a parking lot has many slots.","Many to many: students enrol in many courses, courses have many students."]
items: One to one: a ticket maps to one vehicle.
One to many: a parking lot has many slots.
Many to many: students enrol in many courses, courses have many students.

blocks.content: 7. Direction of a Relationship
A relationship can be one way or two way. Decide who needs to know about whom, and avoid making both sides reference each other unless you truly need it.
For example, a Ticket needs to know its Vehicle, but the Vehicle may not need to know its Ticket. Keeping references one way where possible keeps the design simpler.

blocks.title: Avoid needless back references
blocks.content: Two classes each holding the other creates tight coupling and update headaches. Only make it two way when both sides genuinely need it.
8. Dependency: A Lighter Link
Sometimes one class simply needs another briefly, for example as a method parameter, without storing it at all. This is a dependency, the lightest relationship of all.
A dependency says "I use this for a moment", not "I own or hold this". Recognising it keeps you from storing references you do not need.
9. A Worked Example: Parking Lot Relationships
blocks.text: 9. A Worked Example: Parking Lot Relationships

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972225284-334397697.png
Let us connect the parking lot entities using everything above.

["ParkingLot has many Levels: composition, a list.","Level has many Slots: composition, a list.","Ticket has one Vehicle and one Slot: association, single references.","Car and Truck are Vehicles: inheritance, is a.","PricingService depends on Ticket: a dependency, not stored."]
items: ParkingLot has many Levels: composition, a list.
Level has many Slots: composition, a list.
Ticket has one Vehicle and one Slot: association, single references.
Car and Truck are Vehicles: inheritance, is a.
PricingService depends on Ticket: a dependency, not stored.

blocks.content: In a few lines, the pile of entities has become a connected design that reads like the real world it models.
10. Sketching Relationships
When you draw a quick diagram, a few simple conventions help the interviewer follow along. You do not need formal notation, just clear arrows.
["A plain line or arrow for association and dependency.","A line for has a relationships, noting one or many.","An arrow pointing to the parent for inheritance."]
items: A plain line or arrow for association and dependency.
A line for has a relationships, noting one or many.
An arrow pointing to the parent for inheritance.

blocks.content: A rough sketch that shows who connects to whom is worth far more than perfect notation nobody reads.
11. A Second Example: Library Relationships
Apply the two questions to a library to prove they are universal.
["A Library has many BookCopies: composition","A Loan has one Member and one BookCopy: association","A BookCopy is linked to one Book: association","A Member has many Loans: one to many, a list"]
items: A Library has many BookCopies: composition
A Loan has one Member and one BookCopy: association
A BookCopy is linked to one Book: association
A Member has many Loans: one to many, a list

blocks.content: Same two questions, is a and has a, turned a second set of entities into a clean design in seconds.
12. Optional Relationships
Sometimes a relationship is not always present. A ticket may not yet have a payment, or a slot may have no vehicle. These optional links are normal and worth noting.

blocks.title: Handle the empty case
blocks.content: When a reference can be absent, decide clearly what empty means, such as a free slot holding no vehicle, and handle it so your code never assumes it is always there.
13. Relationships and Clean Extension
Good relationships make a design easy to extend. When entities depend on abstractions rather than concrete classes, adding a new type does not disturb the existing ones.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.text: If ParkingLot holds a PricingStrategy interface rather than a specific pricing class, adding a new pricing rule is a new class, and the relationship stays untouched. Clean relationships are what make the Open Closed principle possible.

blocks.content: The quality of your relationships decides how gracefully your design grows. Loose, sensible links bend. Tight, tangled ones break.
14. Common Mistakes

{"pros":["Ask is a or has a for each pair","Prefer composition over inheritance","Note the multiplicity, one or many","Keep references pointing the sensible way"],"cons":["Overusing inheritance for everything","Deep, fragile inheritance chains","Forgetting whether it is one or many","Two classes needlessly referencing each other"]}
15. Common Questions
When should I use inheritance versus composition? - Use inheritance only for a true is a relationship. For everything else, prefer composition, which is more flexible and avoids fragile hierarchies.

What is the difference between aggregation and composition? - Both are has a. In composition the part dies with the whole, like rooms in a house. In aggregation the part lives on its own, like players in a team.
Do I need to get multiplicity exactly right? - Get the common cases right, especially one versus many, because that decides whether you store a single object or a list.
What is a dependency versus an association? - An association stores a reference for ongoing use. A dependency just uses another class briefly, often as a method parameter, without storing it.
16. Key Takeaways

items: Relationships turn a list of entities into a real design.
Ask is a or has a for every pair of entities.
Association, aggregation, and composition are all forms of has a, differing in ownership.
Use inheritance only for a genuine is a, and prefer composition when unsure.
Multiplicity, one or many, decides single reference versus list.
Keep references one way where possible to reduce coupling.

blocks.content: With entities identified and connected, you have a working class map. Next you will apply design principles to keep each class clean and each responsibility in the right place.
